analysis.one_liner: Repeals regulators' duty to evaluate banks' community-lending records and limits fair-lending enforcement.
analysis.headline: A House bill that would have gutted the Community Reinvestment Act and made lending-discrimination cases harder to win never got a vote, dying in subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the part of the Community Reinvestment Act requiring bank regulators to check whether a bank is meeting the credit needs of its whole community, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. It would have replaced that check with a requirement that banks simply publish a written description of their community lending programs. It also would have added an explicit ban on 'redlining' — refusing credit based on the racial or ethnic makeup of a neighborhood — while sharply weakening enforcement: it would have limited the Attorney General's power to sue creditors on his own authority, and barred courts from using statistics showing a lender's decisions hit certain groups harder unless someone also proved intentional discrimination.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and mortgage lenders. They would be freed from having their community-lending records weighed when they seek approval for new branches or mergers, gain protection from lawsuits built on statistical evidence of discriminatory lending patterns, and face a Justice Department with less power to bring pattern-and-practice cases on its own initiative. The explicit redlining ban added a small new legal duty, but the enforcement changes cut far more in lenders' favor.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the requirement that federal regulators evaluate a financial institution's record of meeting the credit needs of its entire community and take that record into account when judging applications for a deposit facility, replacing it with a public written disclosure of the bank's community lending activities [S2][S3].

Adds an explicit prohibition on creditors discriminating based on the racial or ethnic characteristics of the neighborhood surrounding an applicant's home or business, under both the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and the Fair Housing Act [S2][S3].

Restricts the Attorney General from initiating civil enforcement actions under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act except on referral, and strikes the Fair Housing Act provision authorizing the Attorney General to sue on his own authority [S2][S3].

Bars statistical evidence of disparate impact from being used to prove a pattern of discriminatory lending unless it is accompanied by additional evidence of actual discrimination and intent to discriminate [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Residents of low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, and borrowers who face discrimination. Without regulator scrutiny of community-lending records, banks would face less pressure to lend in less affluent areas, and the higher evidentiary bar would make it much harder to prove discriminatory lending patterns in court — the people harmed by such patterns would bear the cost.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the community-lending evaluation leaves only a self-reported public description of a bank's lending programs, with no regulatory consequence if a bank neglects low- and moderate-income neighborhoods [S2][S3].

Requiring proof of intent before statistical evidence of disparate impact can be used would make pattern-and-practice discrimination cases far harder to win, since discriminatory lending often shows up in outcomes rather than stated intent [S2][S3].

A good-faith objection supporters would raise: routine CRA examinations impose paperwork and can influence bank merger approvals, and some argued credit decisions should be judged on intent, not statistical outcomes. The bill's added explicit redlining ban and disclosure requirement were offered as protections, though they were weaker than the enforcement tools removed [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered banks substantial relief from community-lending scrutiny and litigation risk, and added an explicit redlining ban and a disclosure requirement. But the protections it added were far weaker than the enforcement tools it removed: regulators would no longer weigh a bank's community-lending record at all, the Justice Department would lose independent authority to sue, and statistical proof of discrimination would be nearly unusable. On balance, the costs to neighborhood access to credit and to fair-lending enforcement outweighed the administrative relief for banks.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Banking and Financial Services and Judiciary Committees, sent to subcommittees in June and July 1995, and never received a hearing or vote before the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill McCollum introduced the Credit Opportunity Amendments Act of 1995 on May 24, 1995, with introductory remarks [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the Committee on Banking and Financial Services and, additionally, to the Judiciary Committee [S5].
On June 2, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and on July 18, 1995, to the Subcommittee on the Constitution [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in either chamber, and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1][S5].
The bill attracted only one cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Residents of low- and moderate-income neighborhoods and borrowers protected by fair-lending laws are better off, because the Community Reinvestment Act's evaluation requirement and the Justice Department's independent enforcement authority were not repealed. Banks that would have gained relief from community-lending scrutiny and disparate-impact lawsuits did not get it.

for.name: Rep. Bill McCollum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor [S1][S5].

for.name: Sole cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only additional support it attracted [S4].

against.name: House Banking and Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it sat in the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit and never came to a markup or vote [S5].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on the Constitution in July 1995 and took no further action [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican with a single Republican cosponsor and died without a vote, so no recorded roll calls show the partisan split; the Congress's banking-deregulation agenda of the era ran along Republican lines.

industries.note: The bill would have freed lenders from having their community-lending records weighed in regulatory approvals, limited the Justice Department's ability to sue them, and barred statistical evidence of discriminatory lending patterns unless intent was proven. Ordinary people in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods would bear the cost through reduced access to credit and weaker recourse against discrimination.
